topic: Delhi HC: a daughter-in-law's right to live in the shared household is not absolute and must be balanced with senior citizens' right to live in peace - Divisional Commissioner's eviction order under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 upheld in principle but modified so the right to residence is not illusory: she picks a home (2 bedrooms, drawing room, kitchen) within four weeks, in-laws pay rent up to Rs 35,000 a month plus deposit, brokerage and shifting, six months' rent in advance, vacate two weeks after; rent continues until her residence right is decided in DV/matrimonial proceedings; default for two months lets her seek restoration; S. Vanitha and Satish Chander Ahuja referred to (Namrata Yadav v. Ramesh Kumar Yadav & Ors., W.P.(C) 12654/2026, 2026 LiveLaw (Del) 1113, Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma, 19 Nov 2026, reported 20-22 Nov 2026)

slides.kicker: Delhi High Court · Family & Senior Citizens
slides.title: In-laws want peace. Wife needs a **roof**.
slides.subtitle: A daughter-in-law can be asked to move out of elderly in-laws' home, but only with a **real, assured home** to go to.
slides.cite: **Namrata Yadav v. Ramesh Kumar Yadav & Ors.** · W.P.(C) 12654/2026 · Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma · 19 November 2026

slides.label: What happened
slides.title: Elderly in-laws **sought eviction**
bullets: The woman had lived in her in-laws' Delhi house since her **2008** marriage, with her son, now in **Class XII**. Her husband had moved out years ago.
The in-laws, aged about **70 and 64**, alleged harassment and applied under the **Senior Citizens Act, 2007** to have her removed.
The DM refused. On appeal, the Divisional Commissioner ordered her to leave within about **three weeks** once alternate housing was given.

slides.label: What the Court said
slides.title: Two rights, **balanced**
bullets: A daughter-in-law's right to live in the **shared household** under the DV Act is real, but **not absolute**.
Senior citizens also have a right to live **peacefully and with dignity**. The finding that living together was unworkable was a **plausible** view.
So the eviction was right in principle, but the order was too vague. A right to residence **cannot be left illusory**.
slides.note: **Law fact:** The DV Act gives a woman a right to **secure residence**. It does not always mean a right to stay in the **in-laws' own property**.

slides.label: The new conditions
slides.title: A **proper home** first
bullets: She picks a home with **2 bedrooms, a drawing room and a kitchen** within **four weeks**, preferably near her son's school.
In-laws pay rent up to **Rs 35,000 a month**, plus deposit, brokerage and shifting costs, with **six months' rent in advance**. She moves two weeks later.
Rent continues until her residence right is **finally decided** in the DV or matrimonial case. If they default for two months, she can seek **restoration**.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: Not a rule for **every family**
bullets: This does **not** mean in-laws can throw out a daughter-in-law whenever they want. Facts and proof matter in each case.
It also does **not** mean she can insist on staying in their house no matter what. Courts look for a **fair balance**.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.

caption:
Can elderly in-laws ask their daughter-in-law to leave their home? The Delhi High Court says yes, but not onto the street 🏠⚖️

A woman had lived in her in-laws' Delhi house since her marriage in 2008, along with her son, who is now in Class XII. Her in-laws, aged about 70 and 64, alleged harassment and moved the authorities under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007. The District Magistrate refused eviction, but the Divisional Commissioner allowed it, giving her roughly three weeks to move once alternate housing was arranged.

Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma said a daughter-in-law's right to live in the shared household under the Domestic Violence Act is not absolute, and must be weighed against senior citizens' right to live in peace and dignity. The eviction was correct in principle, but the order was too vague to protect her right to a home.

So the Court set clear terms: she chooses a two-bedroom home within four weeks, the in-laws pay rent up to Rs 35,000 a month plus deposit, brokerage and shifting costs, with six months' rent in advance, and she moves two weeks after that. The rent continues until her right of residence is finally decided in the DV or matrimonial case.

Case: Namrata Yadav v. Ramesh Kumar Yadav & Ors., W.P.(C) 12654/2026, 2026 LiveLaw (Del) 1113
Court: Delhi High Court, Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma (19 November 2026)
